GeoInv3D · field-data test · 28 September 2026

Karnataka Gravity Inversion: Comparing Regularizations

The same Bouguer gravity data on the same mesh, inverted at full resolution on AWS EC2 with six regularization settings. This report compares their data fit, lateral structure and depth, cross-checks them against the 24 September SimPEG run on an 8 km deep mesh and against Tomofast-x, and tests whether a coarse 2 km study can stand in for full-resolution runs.

Area
70 × 70 km, easting 641–711 km, northing 1634–1704 km (UTM 43N, EPSG:32643)
Data
NGPM Bouguer anomaly, 500 m grid decimated to 1 km: 5,040 points; second-order trend surface removed
Mesh
1 km × 1 km × 500 m core, 10 km deep; about 20 km padding at the sides and bottom (factor 1.3): 84 × 84 × 27 = 190,512 cells
Runs
6 full-resolution inversions on AWS EC2 (ap-south-1), 2 of them submitted from the upload page; a 16-run 2 km study run locally

Summary

  • All six runs fit the data about equally well. χ²/N 0.86–1.08, residual RMS 0.46–0.52 mGal. The fit alone cannot choose between these models.
  • The lateral structure is robust. The vertically integrated density maps correlate at 0.83–0.98 pairwise, and at no less than 0.89 without the original settings. The NW–SE dense belt and the low-density belts to the east have the same position and strike in every model.
  • The regularization sets the depth. Centroid depth under the main Bouguer high: 3.4 km for β = 0.5, 3.8 km for L1–L2, 5.6 km for β = 1, 6.4 km for αs = 0.1 and 7.6 km for β = 1.5. The original settings give a column from the surface to the bottom of the mesh (19.9 km). A larger β gives a deeper model with no matching change in χ²/N.
  • A different set-up gives the same depth. The 24 September SimPEG run on an 8 km deep mesh (αs = 0.05, sensitivity weighting) put the main body at 3.3–7.3 km (half maximum), centroid 5.3 km; this report's β = 1 run gives 3.3–7.8 km and 5.6 km. Tomofast-x fitted the data more closely (chi 0.65) but its model has no base, and it took about 2.7 hours against SimPEG's 9 minutes.
  • The coarse 2 km study is good for screening. For three values of β it predicted the full-resolution centroid of the main body to within 0.6 km; for αs = 0.1 it was 1.5 km off. A coarse run takes about 25 s, a full-resolution run about 5 minutes.
  • Recommendation. αs = 1 (now the pipeline default) with Li & Oldenburg depth weighting, β between 0.5 and 1, reporting a range of depths rather than a single model: β = 0.5 agrees with L1–L2, β = 1 with the 8 km deep mesh.
  • Caveat. Gravity data alone do not determine depth; the depths in this report are a consequence of the regularization. The actual depths need constraints from rock densities, geological sections or seismic data.

1Data and the runs compared

Within the area the Bouguer anomaly ranges from −94.9 to −44.3 mGal. Its main feature is a NW–SE trending high from (650, 1685) to (675, 1660) km. After removing a least-squares second-order trend surface (the regional field, −95.3 to −75.9 mGal), the residual anomaly ranges from −16.4 to +31.7 mGal; this is what was inverted (Figure 1). Every point was given an error of 0.5 mGal. Bouguer data are positive downward and SimPEG's gz is positive upward, so the pipeline multiplies the data by −1 before the inversion and returns the observed and predicted data in the original convention.

The six runs share the mesh, the data and the errors; only the regularization differs:

Common settings: density contrast bounded to −0.2 to +0.5 g/cc (rock samples 2.52–3.40 g/cc, median 2.66); β chosen automatically for χ² = N; at most 30 iterations and 30 IRLS iterations. αx = αy = αz = 1, passed to SimPEG as length scales. Li & Oldenburg depth weighting weights the model norm by (z + z₀)−β/2, where z is the depth below the nearest station and z₀ half the smallest cell.

2Comparing the full-resolution results

2.1Data fit

All six runs reached the target fit, with nearly the same statistics. The residual maps (Figure 2) differ, though:

  • Original settings: the residuals cluster at a few places with steep gradients, as patches of positive and negative misfit up to 7.7 mGal. A model made of columns struggles to fit adjacent narrow anomalies.
  • L1–L2: a broad positive residual over the main high, negative around it: the model underestimates the amplitude of the main anomaly (its main body is at the +0.5 g/cc bound). Its χ²/N is also the highest (1.08).
  • The four depth-weighted runs: the least structured residuals, mostly short-wavelength stripes along strike and a few isolated points. The isolated points near (660, 1680) and (702, 1659) km appear in every model and are probably outliers from the original gridding.

2.2Lateral structure

Figure 3 shows five models at 1.8, 4.8 and 7.8 km depth. The top row of Figure 4 shows the vertically integrated density (the sum of density contrast × thickness in each column), the bottom row the centroid depth of each column.

  • The integrated density maps are nearly the same. Pairwise correlations are 0.83–0.98, and no less than 0.89 without the original settings (table below). The NW–SE dense belt, the secondary high at its north-western end and the parallel low-density belts to the east have the same position and strike in every model.
  • What differs is the amplitude and sharpness. A larger β gives stronger integrated density and sharper edges; the original settings give the smoothest model.
  • The centroid depth maps are completely different. For the same dense belt the centroid lies at 2–4 km for β = 0.5 and L1–L2, 4–6 km for β = 1, 6–8 km for β = 1.5 (locally below 12 km), and deeper than 10 km for the original settings.
  • The slices show the same thing. For β = 0.5 there is no anomaly left at 7.8 km; for β = 1.5 only scattered fragments remain at 1.8 km; the original model is almost the same at all three depths.

2.3Depth

Figure 5 shows an E–W section through the main Bouguer high (northing 1664.5 km), and the left panel of Figure 6 the distribution of |mass| with depth below the core area. The table gives where the mass lies, and measures of the density profiles under the main Bouguer high (easting 671.5 km, northing 1664.5 km) and the north-western high (650.5, 1682.5 km).

Depth is given as the centroid (the mean depth of the positive density contrast, weighted by thickness) rather than the depth of the peak: with αs = 1 the main body reaches the +0.5 g/cc bound, so the peak is a plateau with no single depth. The half-maximum range is the depth interval where the density exceeds half the peak.

Core, lateral padding and below 10 km add up to 100%. D50, D90: half and 90% of the |mass| below the core area lie above this depth. Red: lateral padding > 20%, below 10 km > 30%, D50 > 7 km, or the main body reaching below 12 km. The 8 km deep mesh is a different mesh, so only the profile measures are comparable.

  • The original settings give columns. Under the main high the density contrast is only 0.15 g/cc and extends from 0.3 to 19.9 km, centroid 10.1 km; 50% of the mass lies below 10 km and 26% in the lateral padding.
  • The other five have a base. The main body ends above 12 km, and at least 80% of the mass lies in the core (60% for β = 1.5).
  • β controls the depth monotonically. For β = 0.5, 1 and 1.5 the centroid of the main body is at 3.4, 5.6 and 7.6 km, the half-maximum range 2.3–4.8, 3.3–7.8 and 4.3–11.1 km, while χ²/N is 0.90, 0.96 and 0.86, unrelated to depth. This is the non-uniqueness of gravity inversion: the data cannot choose β.
  • L1–L2 is nearly the same as β = 0.5. Two quite different regularizations give the same half-maximum range (2.3–4.8 km), with centroids 0.4 km apart.
  • αs = 0.1 lies between β = 1 and β = 1.5. Centroid 6.4 km, peak 0.48 g/cc, close to but not at the bound. The model is smoother than with αs = 1; the north-western high extends from 0.3 to 4.8 km.
  • β = 1.5 starts to trail to depth. The low-density body in the east reaches 20 km (Figure 5), and 33% of the mass lies below 10 km.
  • The north-western high is always shallower. Apart from the original settings, its centroid lies at 1.6–3.5 km, 1.7–4.1 km above that of the main high. This relation holds in every model.

The radially averaged power spectrum of the residual anomaly (Figure 7) has three straight segments, giving mean depths to the top of the sources of 6.0, 2.2 and 1.1 km (Spector & Grant). It shows sources at several depths but cannot choose between the models: the top of the main body for β = 0.5 and L1–L2 (2.3 km) is near the intermediate estimate, the centroid for β = 1 (5.6 km) near the deep one. Spectral depths are averages over an ensemble of sources and are very uncertain.

2.4What is robust

The same under every setting:

  • The lateral position, strike and extent of the anomalous bodies: the NW–SE dense belt and the low-density belts to the east.
  • Sign and relative strength: the strongest positive body lies under the main Bouguer high.
  • The main body has a base (in the five models other than the original settings, and in the independent 8 km deep mesh run); the north-western high is shallower than the main high.

Changes with the regularization:

  • Absolute depth: the centroid of the main body lies at 3.4–7.6 km depending on β.
  • Thickness and density contrast: with αs = 1 the main bodies reach the +0.5 / −0.2 g/cc bounds. This blocky, saturated model is a product of the regularization, not a measurement of density.
  • Deep details, such as the low-density body in the east reaching 20 km for β = 1.5.

χ²/N (0.86–1.08) cannot be used to choose between these models.

3Cross-check: SimPEG on an 8 km deep mesh, and Tomofast-x

On 24 September the same Karnataka gravity data were inverted with two independent codes: SimPEG, used throughout this project, and Tomofast-x 2.0, an open-source parallel code. Both used the same 8 km deep mesh (500 m horizontal and 250 m vertical cells), the same cloud machine (16 vCPU, 123 GB memory) and the same noise model. Only the gravity part is summarised here; for magnetics see the original report (Desktop/Tomofastx_vs_SimPEG_package).

SimPEGTomofast-x 2.0
Data fit, chi1.040.65
Data used4,900 points (every second node)19,600 points (all)
Under the main Bouguer high3.3–7.3 km at half maximum, centroid 5.3 km, peak 0.64 g/cc; 0.03 g/cc at 9.2 km, while the mesh reaches 14.4 kmNo base: the 1st, 50th and 99th percentiles of each layer change by less than 10% from the surface to 8 km
RegularizationChosen once: sparse, norms (0, 2, 2, 1), αs = 0.05, sensitivity-based depth weighting24-trial search of two smoothing weights; still no shape
Time to the final model9 minutes (522 s)About 2.7 hours (1.7 h search + 1.0 h full run)

How it relates to this report

  • Why the 24 September SimPEG model has a base. It used αs = 0.05. With length-scale alphas the smallness term is then about a fifth of the gradient terms, so the compactness constraint acts; the original settings in this report used αs = 10⁻⁴, about 2500 times weaker, and gave columns (Section 5).
  • Two different set-ups give the same depth. The 8 km mesh (500 m cells, sensitivity weighting, 4,900 data) gives 3.3–7.3 km with the centroid at 5.3 km; the 1 km tensor mesh with αs = 1 and β = 1 (5,040 data) gives 3.3–7.8 km and 5.6 km (Figure 9). The north-western high agrees too (centroid 3.1 against 2.8 km). The result is therefore not sensitive to the mesh or the thinning, but both are the same kind of depth-weighted compact SimPEG model and do not remove the non-uniqueness: β = 0.5 and L1–L2 are shallower, β = 1.5 deeper, and the data cannot tell them apart.
  • A good chi is not evidence of a good model. Tomofast-x reached chi 0.65, below the target, with no vertical shape at all; this report's β sweep also shows models with nearly the same chi whose depths differ by a factor of two. A settings search that looks only at chi selects physically meaningless settings. A published Tomofast-x application (Bird et al., 2025, Antarctic bathymetry) reached the same conclusion and ran 72 full-length trial inversions instead.

Cost (gravity only)

StageApprox. time
SimPEG gravity, final run (8 km mesh, 16 vCPU)9 minutes (522 s)
Tomofast-x gravity: 24-trial settings search1.7 hours
Tomofast-x gravity: full-length run1.0 hour
SimPEG (this report, EC2 c5.2xlarge, 1 km mesh)5–6 minutes per run, about $0.03

Most of Tomofast-x's cost comes from one feature: it does not tune its own regularization, so its two smoothing weights must be found before a run by repeated trials, each 12–17 minutes on the full problem. SimPEG adjusts β during the run and needs no search.

What this does not show

  • SimPEG used less data: 4,900 points against Tomofast-x's 19,600. Tomofast-x handles the full data volume with a wavelet-compressed sensitivity matrix, a real strength this comparison does not credit.
  • SimPEG had its own problems: two faults in the workflow at the time (a mesh-depth setting that had no effect, a missing solver speed-up) took hours to find. They are fixed, but the time is not in the table.
  • Tomofast-x can converge here: on a shallower 3 km mesh it reached an on-target fit (gravity chi 1.87) with a search. The failure is in producing a bounded body at depth, not in fitting the data.
  • We may not have used Tomofast-x well: its published applications also use bound constraints and other controls that we did not try. Its smoothness term cannot be made "blocky" as SimPEG's can, our best explanation for the copied-downward pattern, but that is a hypothesis and was not tested further.
  • One dataset, one operator: a single survey handled by one person new to Tomofast-x.

Trends on the coarse mesh

  • αs decides whether the model reaches the bottom of the mesh. With sensitivity weighting, αs = 10⁻⁴, 10⁻², 0.1 and 1 leave 50%, 45%, 34% and 22% of the mass below 10 km.
  • Depth weighting decides the lateral leakage. With αs = 1, sensitivity weighting puts 33% of the mass in the lateral padding, depth weighting only 5%–10%.
  • β sets the mean depth. β = 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 give D50 = 1.9, 4.6, 6.8 and 8.9 km and main-body centroids of 2.8, 5.8, 7.5 and 9.7 km. The β = 2 often used for gravity is the deepest here, with 54% of the mass below 10 km.
  • The norms matter less. With αs = 1 and β = 1, p = [0,2,2,2], [0,2,2,1] and [0,1,1,1] give main-body centroids of 5.8, 6.1 and 6.0 km.

Against the 1 km runs

At the same place (Figure 10), for the three values of β the coarse centroid is within 0.6 km of the 1 km result and the base within 0.5 km; the top is shallower on the coarse mesh (0.5 against 2.3 km for β = 0.5) because its cells are 1 km thick. αs = 0.1 is the exception: on the coarse mesh the body does not saturate (peak 0.20 g/cc), spans 0.5–8.5 km, and its centroid is 1.5 km shallower than at 1 km. The coarse mesh is good for screening β and comparing trends; the final result should still be confirmed at full resolution.

5Why the original settings give columns

The original settings were sparse (IRLS), p = [0, 2, 2, 1], αs = 10⁻⁴, αx = αy = αz = 1 (length scales), with sensitivity weighting. There are three reasons:

  1. The smallness term does almost nothing. The pipeline passes αx,y,z to SimPEG as length scales, so the gradient terms are weighted by (1 × 500 m)², about 0.25 Δm² per cell, some 2500 times stronger than the 10⁻⁴ m² of the smallness term; the compactness constraint ps = 0 therefore has almost no effect.
  2. L1 on the vertical gradient. pz = 1 favours models that are piecewise constant with depth, so a column that does not change with depth costs almost nothing.
  3. Sensitivity weighting makes the padding cheap. Cells outside the area and at depth have low sensitivity and therefore low weights, so mass placed there costs little (26% went into the lateral padding).

The 2 km study separates the three: changing only the depth weighting (base_dw1, αs still 10⁻⁴) leaves 49% of the mass below 10 km; changing only pz to 2 (as1e-4_p0222) leaves 49%; changing only αs to 1 brings it down to 22%, and αs = 1 with depth weighting to 15%. The first reason dominates. The pipeline default is now αs = 1.

6Recommendations

  1. Default settings: sparse, αs = 1, p = [0,2,2,2] or [0,2,2,1], depth weighting depth with β between 0.5 and 1. Report the β = 0.5 and β = 1 models together as a depth range (main-body centroid about 3.4–5.6 km), with L1–L2 as an independent check.
  2. Coarse first, then fine: screen settings on the 2 km mesh, confirm on the 1 km mesh. The upload page's parameter sweep submits several β at once and compares them in one workflow.
  3. Separate the robust from the rest when interpreting: lateral position, strike and relative strength can be interpreted directly; depth, thickness and density contrast need independent constraints.
  4. Constrain depth with independent data: rock densities, geological sections, boreholes or seismic data; or a gravity synthetic model resembling this area, to check which β recovers a known depth.
  5. Data: remove isolated outliers or use a robust misfit, and check whether the 0.5 mGal noise floor is appropriate.
  6. Tomofast-x: worth considering only where SimPEG exceeds memory even after thinning, or for joint gravity–magnetic inversion. If it is used, run full-length trials (not short proxies) and check the recovered depth profile, not chi alone.
